title: Lists
short: The everyday container: add, remove, index, slice, copy.
what: A list keeps values in order, numbered from 0. It grows and shrinks at the end cheaply. Changing the front or the middle means shifting everything after it.
analogy: A row of numbered lockers. Adding one at the end is easy. Squeezing one in at the front means everyone moves down a locker.

frames.label: nums = [3, 8, 5]
frames.say: nums = [3, 8, 5]. Indexes start at 0: nums[0] is 3, nums[2] is 5, and len(nums) is 3.

frames.label: nums.append(1)
frames.say: nums.append(1) adds to the end. Nothing else moves, so it takes the same tiny time however long the list is.

frames.label: negative index
frames.say: nums[-1] is the last item, nums[-2] the one before it. No len(nums) - 1 arithmetic needed.

frames.label: nums.insert(0, 9)
frames.say: nums.insert(0, 9) puts 9 at the front. Every other item shifts one place right, so it costs O(n).

frames.label: nums.pop()
frames.say: nums.pop() removes the last item and returns it. O(1). pop(0) also works but shifts everything left: O(n).

frames.label: nums[1:3]
frames.say: nums[1:3] copies from index 1 up to, but not including, 3. A slice is a new list.

frames.label: 8 in nums
frames.say: 8 in nums checks the items one by one until it meets 8. Fine once, slow inside a loop: O(n) each time.

frames.label: b = nums; c = nums[:]; nums.append(7)
frames.out: b ends in 7, c does not
frames.say: b = nums copies nothing: both names point at one list, so b sees the new 7. c = nums[:] is a real copy and does not.

when: Use it as a stack: append and pop
Take a piece with a slice
python:
nums = [3, 8, 5]
nums.append(1)
print(nums, len(nums), nums[-1])
nums.insert(0, 9)
print(nums.pop(), nums)
print(nums[1:3], nums[::-1], 8 in nums)
b = nums
c = nums[:]
nums.append(7)
print(b, c)
watch: nums[len(nums)] raises IndexError. The last index is len(nums) - 1, or -1.
b = nums shares one list. Copy with nums[:] or list(nums).
pop(0) in a loop is O(n²). For a queue, use collections.deque.
